world_vegan_day.label: World Vegan Day
world_vegan_day.intro: A day for plant-based cooking and for everyone curious about it. Markets, cafés and kitchens show off what happens when meat, milk and eggs simply stay out of the recipe.
funFacts: Donald Watson coined the word vegan in 1944 by taking the first three and last two letters of vegetarian.
The date marks the fiftieth birthday of the UK Vegan Society, celebrated for the first time in November 1994.
Aquafaba, the liquid from a tin of chickpeas, whips up like egg white and turns into meringue.

deviled_egg_day.label: National Deviled Egg Day
deviled_egg_day.intro: Halved boiled eggs, the yolk mashed with mustard, mayonnaise and a dusting of paprika, then piped back in. A buffet classic that disappears faster than anything else on the table.
funFacts: Stuffed eggs were already served in ancient Rome, seasoned with spicy sauces at the start of a banquet.
In English cooking, deviled has meant highly spiced since the 18th century, long before the eggs got the name.
In parts of the American South they are politely called stuffed or dressed eggs to avoid the word devil.

sandwich_day.label: National Sandwich Day
sandwich_day.intro: The birthday of the man who lent his name to the world's most practical meal: two slices of bread and whatever you like in between. Portable, endlessly variable and never out of fashion.
funFacts: John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich, was born on 3 November 1718; the food was named after him, not the other way round.
The earl took his title from the town of Sandwich in Kent, on the English Channel coast.
The word first appears as a food in a 1762 journal entry by the historian Edward Gibbon.

king_tut_day.label: King Tut Day
king_tut_day.intro: On 4 November 1922, Howard Carter’s team uncovered the first step to Tutankhamun’s tomb. Its exceptionally well-preserved contents captivated the world.
funFacts: Howard Carter's team uncovered the first step on 4 November 1922; the antechamber was opened three weeks later.
Asked whether he could see anything, Carter is said to have answered: Yes, wonderful things.
The tomb held more than 5,000 objects, among them a gold death mask weighing roughly ten kilograms.

guy_fawkes_night.label: Guy Fawkes Night
guy_fawkes_night.intro: Britain's bonfire night: fireworks over the rooftops, sparklers in cold hands and something sticky and sweet to eat. The whole country remembers a plot that famously never came off.
funFacts: The rhyme still learned by heart begins: Remember, remember the fifth of November.
Traditional food includes toffee apples, bonfire toffee and parkin, a sticky ginger cake from northern England.
Lewes in Sussex holds the largest celebrations, with several societies parading through town by torchlight.

saxophone_day.label: National Saxophone Day
saxophone_day.intro: A birthday party for the instrument that gave jazz its voice. Adolphe Sax wanted something that carried like a brass instrument but sang like a woodwind, and he got both.
funFacts: Adolphe Sax was born on 6 November 1814 in Dinant, Belgium, and patented the saxophone in 1846.
Although it is made of brass, the saxophone counts as a woodwind because its sound starts at a single reed.
Sax survived a startling run of childhood accidents, including a fall from a height and swallowing a needle.

bittersweet_chocolate_with_almonds_day.label: National Bittersweet Chocolate with Almonds Day
bittersweet_chocolate_with_almonds_day.intro: Dark chocolate, whole almonds, nothing else needed. The bitter cocoa and the buttery crunch are one of those pairings nobody had to invent twice.
funFacts: In the United States a bar may only be sold as bittersweet if it contains at least 35 percent cacao.
Almonds are not nuts: botanically they are the seed inside a stone fruit, making them close relatives of the peach.
The Aztecs used cacao beans as money; a few beans were enough to buy a meal at market.

cook_something_bold_day.label: Cook Something Bold and Pungent Day
cook_something_bold_day.intro: Permission to reach for the garlic, the chilli and the ripest cheese in the fridge. The idea is a kitchen smell so bold that the whole building knows what is for dinner.
funFacts: The day was thought up by Thomas and Ruth Roy, a couple from Pennsylvania who have registered dozens of odd observances.
Garlic only smells of garlic once it is cut: crushing the cells releases allicin, which is absent in the whole clove.
Durian smells so strongly that it is banned from buses and trains in Singapore, complete with a warning pictogram.

inventors_day.label: Inventors' Day
inventors_day.intro: Germany, Austria and Switzerland mark Inventors’ Day on Hedy Lamarr’s birthday. The film star also co-invented a frequency-hopping system.
funFacts: Hedy Lamarr was born in Vienna on 9 November 1914 and became a Hollywood star in the 1930s.
With composer George Antheil she patented frequency hopping in 1942, an idea later echoed in wireless technology.
The German-language Inventors' Day was launched in 2005 by the Austrian inventor Gerhard Muthenthaler.

area_code_day.label: Area Code Day
area_code_day.intro: The day the telephone learned to find its own way. On this date in 1951 a customer dialled clear across the United States for the first time without asking an operator for help.
funFacts: On 10 November 1951 Englewood's mayor M. Leslie Denning rang his counterpart Frank Osborne in Alameda, California, himself, with no operator in between.
It took three digits of area code plus a seven-digit number, and that ten-digit pattern still holds across North America.
AT&T's first nationwide numbering plan of October 1947 carved North America into 86 area codes, with room for 152.

origami_day.label: Origami Day
origami_day.intro: A square of paper, no scissors, no glue. Japan marks the day with folded cranes, and the same craft turns up in engineering whenever something large has to become small.
funFacts: A senbazuru is a garland of a thousand folded cranes, traditionally given as a wish for health or peace.
Akira Yoshizawa developed the folding notation used worldwide and is said to have created some 50,000 models.
The Miura fold, an origami pattern, has been used to pack solar panels for spacecraft so they open in one pull.

pizza_with_the_works_day.label: National Pizza with the Works Except Anchovies Day
pizza_with_the_works_day.intro: Order everything the kitchen has, then draw one firm line. The longest, most opinionated name on the food-day calendar, and a reliable way to start an argument at the table.
funFacts: The works means every topping on the menu at once, a phrase American diners have used for generations.
Anchovies land at the bottom of almost every survey of favourite pizza toppings in the United States.
The Margherita of 1889 was built the other way round: tomato, mozzarella and basil, and nothing more.

world_kindness_day.label: World Kindness Day
world_kindness_day.intro: A day with one very simple task: do something friendly that nobody asked for. A message, a seat offered, a coffee paid forward — small gestures, deliberately made visible for once.
funFacts: The World Kindness Movement was founded at a Tokyo conference in 1997; the day has been marked since 1998.
In Naples the caffè sospeso is over a century old: you pay for two coffees and leave one for a stranger.
Singapore has had a kindness mascot since 1982, a friendly lion called Singa who campaigns for everyday courtesy.

pickle_day.label: National Pickle Day
pickle_day.intro: Sour, crunchy and impossible to eat quietly. A day for the cucumber that spent a few weeks in brine and came out with far more personality than it went in with.
funFacts: Cucumbers turn into pickles two ways: lactic acid fermentation in salt brine, or a quick bath in hot vinegar.
The Spreewald gherkin from Brandenburg has carried a protected EU geographical indication since 1999.
In the United States the brine is bottled and sold as a sports drink, popular against muscle cramps.

spicy_hermit_cookie_day.label: National Spicy Hermit Cookie Day
spicy_hermit_cookie_day.intro: A soft, dark, heavily spiced bar cookie from New England: molasses, cinnamon, cloves and raisins. Built to keep, which is exactly why sailors loved them.
funFacts: Hermits get their colour and chew from molasses, and their warmth from cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg and ginger.
They keep for weeks and improve after a day or two, so New England crews took them on long voyages.
Recipes turn up in American cookbooks from the late 19th century; where the name comes from is still disputed.

button_day.label: National Button Day
button_day.intro: In praise of the small disc that holds everything together. Collectors sort them by material, age and pattern, and anyone who has ever opened a button tin knows how quickly time passes.
funFacts: The day goes back to the National Button Society, founded in 1938, which made collecting a recognised hobby.
Buttons are around 5,000 years old, but they were ornaments first: the buttonhole only appeared in medieval Europe.
Men's shirts button left over right and women's the other way round; every explanation for it is a theory.

take_a_hike_day.label: National Take a Hike Day
take_a_hike_day.intro: Boots on, phone in the pocket, out of the door. November light, cold air and a marked trail are all it takes — the good part is that any distance counts.
funFacts: The Appalachian Trail runs about 3,500 kilometres; walking it in one go takes most people five to seven months.
The European long-distance path E1 leads roughly 8,000 kilometres from northern Norway down to Sicily.
Germany alone is criss-crossed by around 200,000 kilometres of waymarked hiking trails.

apple_cider_day.label: Apple Cider Day
apple_cider_day.intro: Freshly pressed, cloudy and unfiltered, usually served warm with a stick of cinnamon. In the United States cider is the drink that makes autumn taste like autumn.
funFacts: In the United States cider means unfermented cloudy apple juice; the alcoholic version is called hard cider.
It takes roughly a kilogram and a half of apples to press a single litre of juice.
More than 7,500 apple varieties are grown worldwide, and blending several of them is what gives cider its depth.

carbonated_beverage_with_caffeine_day.label: National Carbonated Beverage with Caffeine Day
carbonated_beverage_with_caffeine_day.intro: A day with a wonderfully bureaucratic name for something very ordinary: the cold, fizzy, faintly buzzing drink in the tall glass with ice.
funFacts: Joseph Priestley worked out how to dissolve carbon dioxide in water in 1767, above a brewery vat in Leeds.
A 330 millilitre glass of cola holds around 35 milligrams of caffeine, roughly a third of a cup of filter coffee.
The tingle of fizzy drinks is not the bubbles but carbonic acid, picked up by the same receptors as sour taste.

absurdity_day.label: National Absurdity Day
absurdity_day.intro: A day set aside for the gloriously pointless. Nonsense, contradictions and ideas that fall apart the moment you think about them — and are all the more enjoyable for it.
funFacts: The critic Martin Esslin coined the term Theatre of the Absurd in 1960 for plays by Beckett, Ionesco and others.
The Ig Nobel Prizes have honoured research since 1991 that first makes you laugh and then makes you think.
Monty Python's Ministry of Silly Walks sketch, first shown in 1970, is still the most-quoted piece of nonsense.

world_hello_day.label: World Hello Day
world_hello_day.intro: The task is charmingly small: greet ten people. The idea behind it is that talking to each other, however briefly, is still the cheapest way to avoid a conflict.
funFacts: Brothers Brian and Michael McCormack started the day in 1973, in response to a war in the Middle East.
People in well over 100 countries now take part, and several Nobel Peace Prize laureates have endorsed it.
Hello owes its career to the telephone: Edison pushed for it, while Alexander Graham Bell preferred Ahoy.

kimchi_day.label: Kimchi Day
kimchi_day.intro: South Korea's fermented cabbage has its own official date. Sharp, salty, alive with lactic acid — and in Korea a side dish so familiar it feels like a member of the household.
funFacts: South Korea made 22 November an official day in 2020: eleven ingredients that unfold twenty-two benefits.
Kimjang, making kimchi together as neighbours and family, joined the UNESCO intangible heritage list in 2013.
Korean kitchens often have a dedicated kimchi fridge, which holds a steady low temperature for the fermentation.

fibonacci_day.label: Fibonacci Day
fibonacci_day.intro: Write the date as 11/23 and you have 1, 1, 2, 3 — the opening of the most famous number sequence there is. Every term is simply the sum of the two before it.
funFacts: Leonardo of Pisa introduced the sequence to Europe in 1202 in Liber Abaci, using a puzzle about breeding rabbits.
As you move along the sequence, each term divided by the previous one approaches the golden ratio, about 1.618.
Count the spirals in a sunflower head or on a pine cone and you usually land on two neighbouring Fibonacci numbers.

evolution_day.label: Evolution Day
evolution_day.intro: On this date in 1859 a book appeared that rearranged the way we see living things. Darwin had been sitting on his idea for twenty years before he finally let it out.
funFacts: On the Origin of Species went on sale on 24 November 1859; the entire first print run was spoken for that same day.
Darwin avoided the noun evolution almost entirely — the first edition simply ends on the word evolved.
The voyage of the Beagle that supplied his material lasted nearly five years, from 1831 to 1836.

parfait_day.label: National Parfait Day
parfait_day.intro: Layer upon layer in a tall glass, and the glass is half the point. Fruit, cream, something crunchy — the French version is frozen, while the American one is often layered with yoghurt or ice cream.
funFacts: Parfait simply means perfect; the French version is a frozen cream dessert made with sugar syrup and egg yolk.
The American parfait is layered instead: yoghurt or ice cream with fruit and granola, served cold in a tall glass.
Parfait glasses are deliberately narrow and high so that every single layer stays visible from the outside.

cake_day.label: National Cake Day
cake_day.intro: No occasion needed today: cake is the occasion. Whether it is a plain sponge or four floors of buttercream, the day exists purely so that a slice can be cut.
funFacts: The English word cake comes from the Old Norse kaka and originally meant a small flat baked good.
Candles on a birthday cake are usually traced back to the German Kinderfeste of the 18th century.
Alfred Bird developed a baking powder in 1843. Before that, bakers could already lighten cakes with yeast or beaten eggs.

electric_guitar_day.label: National Electric Guitar Day
electric_guitar_day.intro: Held on Jimi Hendrix's birthday, in honour of six strings, a pickup and an amplifier. No instrument changed the sound of the last century quite so thoroughly.
funFacts: Jimi Hendrix was born on 27 November 1942 in Seattle; left-handed, he simply restrung a right-handed guitar.
The first commercially successful electric guitar, the 1932 Frying Pan lap steel, was named after a kitchen pan.
Fender launched the Broadcaster in 1950; the name Telecaster followed in 1951.

red_planet_day.label: Red Planet Day
red_planet_day.intro: The date honours the launch of Mariner 4 in 1964, the probe that sent back humanity's first close-up pictures of Mars. Ever since, the fourth planet has felt like a neighbour.
funFacts: Mariner 4 launched on 28 November 1964 and returned 21 complete images and part of a 22nd during its Mars flyby in July 1965.
Mars looks red because its dust is full of iron oxide — the planet is, quite literally, rusty.
Olympus Mons rises about 22 kilometres above the plains around it, the tallest volcano in the solar system.

square_dance_day.label: National Square Dance Day
square_dance_day.intro: Four couples, one square and a caller shouting out the next move. Nobody has to know the choreography in advance, which is exactly what makes it so easy to join in.
funFacts: The dance grew out of English country dances, the French quadrille and Irish and Scottish figures.
A caller announces every figure live, so dancers follow instructions rather than a memorised routine.
Modern square dance calls are given in English worldwide, so a dancer from Japan can join a set in Sweden.

mason_jar_day.label: National Mason Jar Day
mason_jar_day.intro: A glass jar with a screw thread and a sealing lid — an everyday object so well designed that it has barely changed in over 160 years. Today it holds salad, drinks and fairy lights.
funFacts: John Landis Mason patented his screw-neck preserving jar on 30 November 1858.
Patented Nov 30th 1858 was still being moulded into jars decades later, long after the patent had run out.
Mason sold his rights early and earned little from the invention; he died in poverty in New York in 1902.
